CI phases

scripts/ci.mjs

In call order, read out of main(). A fast phase also runs on --fast and in the pre-push hook; the rest only on a full run.

01
hygienefast

Everything here is about the difference between THIS working copy and a fresh clone.

02
structurefast

The architecture rules, run over this repo's own apps and packages with the same engine `fli check` gives a client app.

03
registersfast

The three registers, graded against the rules they state about themselves.

04
snapshotsfast

A snapshot is a generated artefact committed beside its source, so a change nothing else in the repo can see arrives as a diff: the access rules enforced below the API, the DDL every hand-written statement binds to, the JSON Schema three packages validate…

05
accessfast

What did this branch do to who may do what.

06
coveragefast

Skipped is not passed. The aggregate `--filter '*'` walks straight past a package with no `test` script and prints nothing at all about it.

07
registryfast

Scaffolds an app, packs the working tree into it, installs and builds it.

08
scaffoldfast
09
typecheckfast

Two halves: the direction of the ratchet (a git question) and the count itself (each package's own script already answers that, and exits 1 above its ceiling).

10
deployfull run

`fli new` → `fli make:deploy` → `fli deploy:local`: does the deploy pipeline containerise a real app? ~30s and it needs a Docker daemon, so it sits in the full tier rather than the pre-push one.

11
testsfull run

Sequential on purpose: several suites bind ports and start real servers, and interleaved output from four different runners is unreadable when one fails.

S2 — high 8

FJS-377 litestone A @from across a composite-key relation correlates on the first key column alone, so the aggregate is silently wrong 2026-08-21 inferFromFk answers a single reference column — refCol: (Array.isArray(rel.references) ? rel.references[0] : rel.references) ?? idField (parser.js:2992) — and the subquery builder emits one equality from it, from."${fkCol}" = %SELF%."${refCol}" (client.js:961). A relation declaring references: [workspaceId, userId] therefore correlates on workspaceId and drops the rest, and fkCol is rel.fields[0] with the same shape, so a composite foreign key is halved on both sides of the join. Measured on a grid built so each candidate join gives a different answer — memberships (1,10), (1,20), (2,10) holding 3, 5 and 7 notes — which read back 8, 8, 7: the count for every row sharing a workspace. Correct is 3, 5, 7; a join on userId alone would have given 10, 5, 10. Nothing raises it, and that is the cost — the number is plausible, it is a count of real rows, and it answers a question nobody asked. Composite keys are otherwise sound, which is what makes this the trap rather than a known gap: the DDL emits a correct PRIMARY KEY (a, b) (ddl.js:217), findUnique on a partial key throws returned more than one row rather than answering the first match, and update/delete address the full key. This is the one path that silently drops a column, so a schema that works everywhere else fails here alone. The fix is fkCol/refCol as arrays with an AND-joined correlation; refusing a composite @from at parse would also beat the current silence.
